subject: English
passage:
The following text is from George Eliot's 1858 short story "The Trials of Miss Lucy Deane." Mr. Omar Hassan is a newcomer to the town of Hartfield.

It is true, Mr. Hassan was a little proud, a little calculating, a little self-interested, a little superficial and impulsive, a little given to slight exaggerations—But who considers such trivial defects, such moral freckles as these, impediments to entering into the most genteel society! Indeed, the strictest ladies in Hartfield would have been perfectly aware that these characteristics would have created no meaningful distinction between Mr. Omar Hassan and themselves: and since it was clear there was a meaningful distinction—why, it must lie in the possession of some vices from which they were unquestionably free.
prompt: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?

choices.A: The residents of Hartfield had initially viewed Mr. Hassan with suspicion, but they have gradually come to see him as mostly harmless.
choices.B: Although Mr. Hassan actively cultivates a sense of mystery about himself, his background is less interesting than what many residents of Hartfield have been led to believe.
choices.C: Although the residents of Hartfield are generally thought to be welcoming, Mr. Hassan has committed many social blunders that have caused him to be widely disliked.
choices.D: Some residents of Hartfield are determined to disapprove of Mr. Hassan even though the reasons for their dislike are largely groundless.

explanation: Choice D is the best answer because it most accurately captures the passage's main idea: the ironic criticism of Hartfield residents who disapprove of Mr. Hassan despite lacking valid reasons. The narrator catalogs Hassan's flaws as 'trivial defects' and 'moral freckles'—minor blemishes that shouldn't disqualify anyone from society. The irony becomes explicit when the text states that 'the strictest ladies in Hartfield would have been perfectly aware that these characteristics would have created no meaningful distinction between Mr. Omar Hassan and themselves,' meaning Hassan's critics possess the same minor flaws yet still maintain their disapproval based on imagined vices 'from which they were unquestionably free.'
